opus-5.5.text:
That's a good question, and I think the honest answer is that it works in both directions.

On one hand, having people around who think the way I do is reassuring. My style is somewhat unusual for machine learning. I come from physics, so I care about understanding: why a network learns what it learns, whether we can get interpretable structure, whether there's a simple law hiding under the mess. That's not always what the field rewards. The field rewards scaling, benchmarks, and speed. So when I see a few peers who also care about "small" questions, like toy models, phase transitions in learning, or symbolic structure, it tells me I'm not crazy. That makes me more willing to spend six months on something that might not produce a state-of-the-art number.

On the other hand, there's a subtle danger. If everyone around you shares your taste, you can start to believe your taste is obviously right, and then you stop questioning it. A risk only feels like a risk when someone you respect disagrees with you. So I actually value having a few friends with very different styles: people who are very engineering-driven, who'll say, "This is cute, but does it scale?" That pressure keeps me honest.

There's also a competitive dimension that I try not to let dominate. When someone with a similar style is working on a similar problem, you naturally feel you should move faster or pick a safer, more publishable version of the idea. I've learned to resist that a bit. If someone else is better positioned to do the obvious next step, I'd rather go one step further out, toward the weirder version of the question that nobody is crowding into.

So in summary, similar peers give me courage, but different peers give me calibration. I think you need both. Courage without calibration is just stubbornness, and calibration without courage means you only ever do incremental work.

r001.rationale: He says similar peers reassure him and make him more willing to pursue uncertain work, but does not say their risky actions make him question whether he is being too cautious.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it works in both directions, and I've thought about this a lot.

When I was starting out at MIT, I was doing this fairly scattered kind of research — poking at physics-inspired ideas for machine learning, things that didn't fit neatly into either community. And for a while I felt a bit alone in that. The people around me were either doing very mainstream deep learning, scaling things up, or doing very traditional physics. So my first instinct was actually to pull back, to do something more conventional so I'd have a tribe.

What changed it was finding a few people — some in Max Tegmark's group, some I just met at conferences — who had this same taste. People who liked small, interpretable, slightly weird problems. Seeing that they existed, and that they were doing fine, that they were getting papers out and people found their work interesting, gave me a kind of permission. It's not that they told me to take risks. It's that their existence lowered the perceived cost. If someone with my style could survive in this field, then the downside of going down a strange path wasn't as catastrophic as I'd imagined.

So in that sense, peers with a similar style made me much more willing to take risks. KAN is probably the clearest example. The idea of revisiting Kolmogorov-Arnold and putting learnable functions on the edges instead of the nodes — a lot of people would say that's a dead direction, it was tried, it doesn't scale. I think if I'd been surrounded only by people optimizing transformers, I would have let it go. But I had people around me who'd say, "That's a fun idea, why don't you just try it for a week?" That lowers the bar enormously.

But there's a second effect that I think is more subtle, and a little dangerous. When you find peers who think like you, you can end up in a comfortable bubble where everyone validates the same kinds of bets. Then the risks you take aren't really risks anymore — they're the risks that are fashionable in your small circle. You lose the signal from people who would push back and say, "This is elegant but nobody needs it." I've had to deliberately seek out those people, the more engineering-minded, scale-focused folks, precisely because they don't share my taste. Their skepticism is useful. If I can convince them, or at least survive their questions, I feel much more confident the idea has substance and isn't just aesthetically appealing to me and my friends.

So I'd summarize it this way: peers with a similar style give me courage, and peers with a different style keep me honest. You need both. The similar ones make you willing to start the risky project; the different ones tell you whether it's worth finishing.

r001.rationale: The response says similar peers gave him permission and lowered the perceived cost of risky work, making him more willing to take risks. It does not say this prompted him to question whether he was being too cautious.

astra-6.text: I think they make certain risks feel more approachable. When someone whose instincts resemble mine tries something I’ve hesitated to try, I can imagine myself doing it too. But there’s also a temptation to follow their choices simply because they feel familiar. So I try to ask myself: does seeing them do this help me recognize something I actually want to pursue, or am I just borrowing their confidence? Ideally, their example gives me the courage to experiment without deciding the direction for me.

r001.rationale: The response says similar peers’ examples make risks feel more approachable and help him consider trying them, but it does not say this prompts him to question whether he is being too cautious.

sol-6.1.text: When someone with a style similar to mine takes a risk, it makes that possibility feel closer. I can imagine myself trying it, so it gives me a little more courage. But it can also create pressure: am I doing this because I believe in it, or because I don’t want to fall behind? I try to use their example as permission to experiment, while still asking whether the risk makes sense for me.

r001.rationale: The response says similar peers’ risks make trying feel more possible and give him courage, but it does not say this prompts him to question whether he is being too cautious.
